questions.stem: The magnitude of an earthquake is measured using the:

options.option_text: Beaufort scale
Richter scale
Mercalli scale (strictly)
Celsius scale

questions.explanation: Richter scale (Charles F. Richter, 1935) measures magnitude (energy released) — logarithmic: a 7.0 quake releases ~32 times more energy than a 6.0. Modern seismologists increasingly use 'moment magnitude' (Mw) for large quakes. Mercalli scale measures intensity (perceived shaking on the ground at a specific location), with 12 roman-numeral levels. Beaufort scale — wind speed (sailors).

questions.stem: Cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal and affect the east coast of India are called tropical cyclones. On the west coast (Arabian Sea side) their equivalent is:

options.option_text: Hurricane
Cyclone (same term)
Typhoon
Tornado

questions.explanation: The same weather system is called a 'cyclone' in the Indian Ocean / South Pacific, a 'hurricane' in the Atlantic / NE Pacific (the Americas), and a 'typhoon' in the NW Pacific (East Asia). Tornadoes are different — small, intense land-based vortices mainly in the US Midwest. Cyclones are named by the IMD under the WMO regional system (Asani, Biparjoy, Mocha etc.).

questions.stem: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) of India is chaired by the:

options.option_text: President
Prime Minister
Home Minister
Chief Justice of India

questions.explanation: NDMA — established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 — is chaired by the Prime Minister. It lays down policies and guidelines on disaster management. State-level equivalents — SDMA, chaired by the Chief Minister. District-level — DDMA, chaired by the District Collector / DM. The operational arm is NDRF (National Disaster Response Force), a specialised force under the MHA.

questions.stem: The Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004 was triggered by a powerful earthquake off the coast of:

options.option_text: Japan
Sumatra (Indonesia)
Chile
Philippines

questions.explanation: The 9.1-9.3 magnitude undersea megathrust earthquake off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia — 26 December 2004 — produced the deadliest tsunami in recorded history (~230,000 deaths across 14 countries; India's Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Andaman & Nicobar Islands were hit hard). This disaster spurred India to set up ITEWS (Indian Tsunami Early Warning System, INCOIS Hyderabad) operational from 2007.

questions.stem: Which region of India is most vulnerable to landslides?

options.option_text: Coastal Tamil Nadu
Himalayan foothills and Western Ghats
Thar desert
Deccan plateau

questions.explanation: Steep slopes + heavy rainfall + weak / young geology make the Himalayas (Uttarakhand, Himachal, NE hills) and the Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra) India's main landslide zones. The Geological Survey of India publishes a landslide susceptibility map. Major recent events — Kedarnath (2013), Kotrupi-Himachal (2017), Wayanad (2024), Joshimath subsidence (2023).

questions.stem: 'Seismic Zone V' on the Indian earthquake hazard map — the zone of highest risk — includes:

options.option_text: Central MP and Deccan plateau
Kashmir, NE India, parts of Gujarat (Kachchh)
Tamil Nadu and Kerala coasts
Entire Peninsular India

questions.explanation: India's seismic zoning: Zone V (very high — entire NE, Kashmir valley, Kachchh-Gujarat, Andamans), Zone IV (high — Delhi, parts of Uttarakhand, Himachal, western UP), Zone III (moderate), Zone II (low — central and southern peninsula). The 2001 Bhuj earthquake (Mw 7.7, ~20,000 deaths) is a Zone-V example. Modern building codes (IS 1893) require higher earthquake resistance in Zones IV and V.

questions.stem: The Disaster Management Act, which created the framework for NDMA/SDMA/DDMA, was passed in:
questions.explanation: The Disaster Management Act, 2005, was enacted soon after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. It created NDMA (national), SDMA (state) and DDMA (district) bodies, the National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM) for training, and the NDRF (response force). The Act was invoked in the Covid-19 response (March 2020 onwards) to impose lockdowns nationally.

questions.stem: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies a rainfall event as a 'cloudburst' when the precipitation amount is at least:

options.option_text: Rainfall of at least 50 mm occurring within one hour
Rainfall of at least 100 mm occurring within one hour
Rainfall of at least 150 mm occurring within one hour
Rainfall of at least 200 mm occurring within one hour

questions.explanation: IMD defines a cloudburst as rainfall of 100 mm or more in a single hour over a small localised area (roughly 20–30 sq km). Option A (50 mm/hour) is a common mis-recall — that threshold relates to 'heavy rainfall' classification, not a cloudburst. Cloudbursts are most destructive in hilly terrain where they trigger flash floods and debris flows with very little warning time.

questions.stem: Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) — the third tier of India's disaster management structure — is chaired by:

options.option_text: The Superintendent of Police of the respective district
The elected Chairperson of the local Zila Panchayat body
The District Collector or District Magistrate of the district
The Divisional Commissioner of the revenue division concerned

questions.explanation: Section 25 of the DM Act 2005 constitutes the DDMA with the District Collector/District Magistrate as Chairperson. The elected head of the local body (Zila Panchayat Chairperson or Mayor) serves as Co-Chairperson — this is the most common distractor confusion in exams. The SP and Divisional Commissioner have no statutory chairing role in the DDMA structure.

questions.stem: India's National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP), which funds cyclone shelters, coastal embankments, and early warning dissemination networks, was launched with financial assistance from:

options.option_text: Asian Development Bank (ADB), based in Manila, Philippines
World Bank (IBRD), providing concessional project funding
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), New York
International Monetary Fund (IMF), based in Washington DC

questions.explanation: NCRMP was launched in 2010 with World Bank (IBRD) concessional assistance, initially covering Andhra Pradesh and Odisha — India's two most cyclone-prone coastlines. ADB is the most tempting distractor as it also funds large Indian infrastructure projects, but NCRMP is specifically a World Bank-supported scheme. UNDP provides technical cooperation rather than large-scale project financing of this type.

questions.stem: The secondary hazard in which water-saturated, loosely packed soil loses its shear strength during ground shaking and temporarily behaves like a viscous liquid is known as:

options.option_text: Soil subsidence, caused by gradual compaction of underground strata
Soil liquefaction, typically triggered by seismic (earthquake) activity
Soil deflation, caused by wind erosion of fine dry surface particles
Soil creep, the slow downhill movement of a saturated soil mass

questions.explanation: Soil liquefaction occurs when seismic waves cause rapid cyclic shearing of saturated granular soil, momentarily eliminating effective stress between particles so they behave like a fluid — structures sink or tilt dramatically, as witnessed in the 2001 Bhuj earthquake in Gujarat. Subsidence is a slow process from compaction or extraction; soil creep is gravity-driven slope movement unrelated to acute seismic shaking.

questions.stem: The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), India's specialised disaster-response force whose battalions are deployed for relief operations across the country, functions under the control of:

options.option_text: Ministry of Earth Sciences, Government of India
Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, GoI
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), New Delhi

questions.explanation: NDRF was constituted under Section 44 of the Disaster Management Act 2005 and is placed under the Ministry of Home Affairs; its battalions are drawn from CPMFs (CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, AR). Option D is the most tempting trap — NDMA provides policy direction and coordinates disaster response, but administrative control of the NDRF vests with MHA, not NDMA itself.

questions.stem: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, adopted at the UN World Conference in Sendai, Japan, formally replaced which preceding international agreement?

options.option_text: The Yokohama Strategy for a Safer World, 1994–2004
The Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA), 2005–2015
The Rio+20 Outcome Document on Disaster Resilience, 2012
The UNISDR Johannesburg Plan on Risk Reduction, 2002

questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework (2015-2030) directly succeeded the Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA, 2005-2015), which was adopted at Kobe, Japan. Option A (Yokohama Strategy, 1994) is the most dangerous distractor — it was a real and genuine predecessor framework, but it was succeeded by HFA in 2005, not directly by Sendai. Options C and D are fictional documents. Sendai carries 7 global targets including reducing disaster mortality and economic losses substantially by 2030.

questions.stem: For the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) under the Disaster Management Act 2005, the Centre contributes 75% of the corpus for general-category states. For special-category states (North-Eastern, hilly, island territories), the Centre's contribution is:

options.option_text: 75% — identical to the share for general category states
80% — a moderately enhanced share for special category states
90% — a substantially higher share for special category states
100% — the Centre fully funds SDRF for all special category states

questions.explanation: Under SDRF norms, the Centre contributes 75% for general states (state bears 25%), and 90% for special category states — NE states, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, J&K, and island territories (state bears 10%). Option D (100%) is a deliberate overshoot distractor: even special states retain a 10% share to maintain local fiscal accountability. Option B (80%) has no basis in the norms. The higher Centre share compensates for these states' limited own-revenue base and disproportionately high disaster exposure.
